title.en: Kheti the Fire-Spitter: The Serpent That Burns the Damned
title.zh: 噴火之蛇克赫提：焚罪者之蛇

region.en: The Eighth Division of the Book of Gates, Egyptian Other World
region.zh: 埃及冥界《門之書》第八區

texts.period: New Kingdom netherworld books (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II, 1911, ch. XXIV)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 11, 'The Spitting Serpent'

summary.en: In the Eighth Division of the Book of Gates stands the speckled serpent Kheti with seven undulations, in each of which a god stands; his mouth open, he belches a stream of fire into the faces of the enemies of Ra — 'Open thy mouth, distend thy jaws, belch forth thy fire against the enemies of my father, burn up their bodies, and consume their souls' — a monster, Budge shows, modelled on the real spitting cobras of Africa, whose venom Livingstone saw distil for hours from a severed head.
summary.zh: 《門之書》第八區立有斑蛇克赫提，身具七曲，每曲立一神；其口大張，向拉之仇敵噴火焰之流——『張爾口，展爾頜，向吾父之敵噴火，焚其身，以爾口所出之火與爾身之焰滅其魂』——伯奇證其型乃非洲實有之噴毒眼鏡蛇：利文斯頓曾見斷首之蛇歷時數小時仍滴清毒。

sensitivity.note: Ancient netherworld iconography via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In the Eighth Section of the Book of Gates a picture is given of a monster speckled serpent called 'Kheti,' with seven undulations, in each of which stands a god. The mouth of the serpent is open, and through it he belches a stream of fire into the faces of the enemies of Ra, whose arms are tied behind their backs in agonizing positions. Horus says to the serpent: 'Open thy mouth, distend thy jaws, belch forth thy fire against the enemies of my father, burn up their bodies, and consume their souls by the fire which issueth from thy mouth, and by the flames which are in thy body.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 11.

passages.text: It was formerly thought spitting serpents did not exist, and that the Egyptian drawings were the result of the artist's imagination. Livingstone, however, killed a serpent of the species picakholu, which was 8 feet 3 inches long, and was so copiously supplied with venom that it continued to distil clear poison from the fangs for hours after its head was cut off. He says, 'This was probably that which passes by the name of spitting serpent, which is believed to be able to eject the poison into the eyes when the wind favours its forcible expiration.' In the Book Am-Tuat (IXth Division) we also have a group of twelve little serpents, the duty of which was to pour out fire from their bodies, which was to light the dead Sun-god on his way.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XXIV, citing Livingstone, Missionary Travels. / Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 11.

title.en: Serpent Worship: The Snake as God and as Devil
title.zh: 蛇之崇拜：蛇為神亦為魔

region.en: Egypt and the Nile valley (the serpent revered and abhorred)
region.zh: 埃及與尼羅河谷（受敬與被憎之蛇）

texts.period: From the Pyramid Texts of Unas onward (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II, 1911, ch. XXIV)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 13, 'Snake-Worship'

summary.en: The double theology of the serpent: 'the serpent was either a power for good or the incarnation of diabolical cunning and wickedness' — the Book of the Dead names the serpent Ami-hemf that lived on the top of a mountain and was thirty cubits long, and the shipwrecked sailor's conversing serpent had a beard two cubits long; the Egyptians drew two-headed serpents and winged human-headed snakes, while Herodotus and Aristotle themselves believed in 'flying serpents' — and reverence still paid to pythons in Africa, where the Dinka call snakes 'brethren' and wash them with milk.
summary.zh: 蛇之雙重神學：『蛇或為善力，或為魔之狡惡化身』——《亡靈書》載居山頂、長三十肘之蛇阿米-赫姆夫，遇難水手所對談之蛇亦長三十肘、鬚長二肘；埃及人畫雙首蛇與有翼人首蛇，而希羅多德與亞里士多德亦信『飛蛇』——非洲至今敬蟒，丁卡人呼蛇為『兄弟』，以乳洗之、以酥膏之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient serpent-cult evidence via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Egyptians regarded certain kinds of snakes with reverence, and their religious books contain many allusions to them; on the other hand, the mythological writings show that some snakes or serpents were regarded as incarnations of evil. Among these are the serpents the names of which are given in the text of Unas, and several others are mentioned in the Book Am-Tuat and the Book of Gates; but all of them appear to have been regarded as forms of the monster serpent Apep, which was the type of all physical and moral evil. In short, the serpent was either a power for good or the incarnation of diabolical cunning and wickedness.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 13.

passages.text: The Book of the Dead mentions (Chapter CVIII) the serpent Ami-hemf, which lived on the top of a mountain and was thirty cubits long, and the Papyrus Golenischeff also mentions a serpent thirty cubits long, which had a beard two cubits long, and which conversed with the shipwrecked mariner on the enchanted island.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 13.

passages.text: The Egyptians represented certain snakes with a head at each end of the body, and Miss Kingsley mentions one serpent which the natives declared to have 'a head at each end.' The Egyptians drew figures of serpents with human heads and legs, and the wings of a bird, but this is not very remarkable when we remember that even Herodotus and Aristotle believed in 'flying serpents.' Reverence is still paid to the serpent in many parts of Africa. Thus the Dinkas revere pythons, and call snakes in general their 'brethren'; they wash them with milk and anoint them with butter.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 13.

title.en: Osiris Is Moisture: The Black Land and the Black God
title.zh: 奧西里斯即濕氣：黑土與黑神

region.en: Egypt, the black land (Chemia, the pupil of the eye)
region.zh: 埃及黑土之邦（『凱米亞』，目之瞳）

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, secs. XXXIII-XXXVIII

summary.en: The second allegorical reading of the myth: Osiris does not symbolize the Nile only but 'the principle and power of moisture in general', Typhon everything scorching, burning and fiery; hence Osiris is of a black colour, 'for water gives a black tinge to everything with which it is mixed' — the Mnevis Bull of Heliopolis is black like him, 'and even Egypt itself, by reason of the extreme blackness of the soil, is called by them Chemia, the very name which is given to the black part or pupil of the eye'; the sun and moon sail their courses in ships 'because they owe their motion, support, and nourishment to the power of humidity', and Homer and Thales both learned from Egypt 'that water was the first principle of all things.'
summary.zh: 神話之第二寓言讀法：奧西里斯非僅象尼羅，乃『濕氣之原理與權力』，而提豐則為一切灼熱焚燒之物；故奧西里斯色黑——『水使所染皆黑』——赫利奧波利斯之姆內維斯牛亦黑如其主；『埃及因土色至黑，遂名凱米亞（Chemia），即目瞳之黑之稱』；日月不駕車而乘舟行天——『以其行、支與養皆賴濕氣之力』；荷馬與泰勒斯之『水為萬物本原』，皆得自埃及。

sensitivity.note: Ancient philosophical allegoresis via Plutarch (Budge's summaries of secs. XXXIII-XXXVIII); no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Some of the more philosophical priests assert that Osiris does not symbolize the Nile only, nor Typhon the sea only, but that Osiris represents the principle and power of moisture in general, and that Typhon represents everything which is scorching, burning, and fiery, and whatever destroys moisture. Osiris they believe to have been of a black colour, because water gives a black tinge to everything with which it is mixed. The Mnevis Bull kept at Heliopolis is, like Osiris, black in colour, 'and even Egypt itself, by reason of the extreme blackness of the soil, is called by them Chemia, the very name which is given to the black part or pupil of the eye.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch secs. XXXIII-XXXIV (Budge's summary).

passages.text: The Sun and Moon are not represented as being drawn about in chariots, but as sailing round the world in ships, which shows that they owe their motion, support, and nourishment to the power of humidity. Homer and Thales both learned from Egypt that 'water was the first principle of all things, and the cause of generation.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), secs. XXXIII-XXXIV (Budge's summary).

passages.text: The Nile and all kinds of moisture are called the 'efflux of Osiris.' Therefore a water-pitcher is always carried first in his processions, and the leaf of a fir-tree represents both Osiris and Egypt. Osiris is the great principle of fecundity, which is proved by the Pamylia festivals, in which a statue of the god with a triple phallus is carried about.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), sec. XXXVI (Budge's summary).

title.en: The Amulet Chapters: Tet, Vulture, Collar, Sceptre, and Pillow
title.zh: 護符諸章：泰特、禿鷲、項圈、權杖與枕

region.en: Egyptian funerary workshops (the amulet spells of the Book of the Dead)
region.zh: 埃及喪葬作坊（亡靈書護符諸咒）

texts.period: Book of the Dead chs. 155-167, Theban recension (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the amulet chapters of the Book of the Dead

summary.en: The dead man's jewellery was a spell-book in metal and stone: chapters 155-167 formed the spells engraved on the amulets — the Tet (male), the Tet (female), the Vulture, the Collar, the Sceptre, the Pillow, the Pectoral — which 'gave to the deceased the power of Osiris and Isis and other gods, and restored to him his heart, and lifted up his head'; ch. 162 kept heat in the body until the day of resurrection, and ch. 177 raised up the dead body, ch. 178 the spirit-soul.
summary.zh: 亡者之飾物乃金石器上的咒文之書：第一五五至一六七章為刻於護符之咒——男泰特、女泰特、禿鷲、項圈、權杖、枕、胸飾——『使亡者得奧西里斯與伊西斯及他神之力，復得其心，舉起其首』；第一六二章為其體保暖以待復活之日；第一七七章舉起屍身，一七八章舉起靈魂。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary chapters summarized in Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Chaps. 155-160, 166, and 167 formed the spells that were engraved on amulets, i.e. the Tet (male), the Tet (female), the Vulture, the Collar, the Sceptre, the Pillow, the Pectoral, &c., and gave to the deceased the power of Osiris and Isis and other gods, and restored to him his heart, and lifted up his head. Chap. 162 kept heat in the body until the day of the resurrection. Chaps. 175 and 176 gave the deceased everlasting life and enabled him to escape the second death. Chap. 177 raised up the dead body, and Chap. 178 raised up the spirit-soul.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, summary.

title.en: A Homestead in the Fields of Peace: Ani's Petition
title.zh: 安樂田中之家宅：阿尼之祈

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (Papyrus of Ani, the opening hymn to Osiris)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（阿尼紙草，奧西里斯開篇頌）

texts.period: Book of the Dead, opening hymn, 18th Dynasty (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the prayer of the scribe Ani

summary.en: The scribe Ani's wish-list for eternity: 'Grant that I may sail down to Tatu in the form of a living soul, and sail up to Abydos in the form of the Benu bird; that I may go in and come out without being stopped at the pylons of the Lords of the Other World. May there be given unto me bread-cakes in the house of coolness, and offerings of food in Anu (Heliopolis), and a homestead for ever in Sekhet Aru, with wheat and barley therefor.'
summary.zh: 書吏阿尼之永恆清單：『願我化為活魂下行至塔圖，化為貝努鳥上行至阿拜多斯；願我於冥界諸主之牌樓前出入無阻。願涼宅中賜我餅，赫利奧波利斯賜我食，而於蘆葦之田賜我永宅，並其大小麥之田。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary prayer via Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Grant thou to the Ka of the Osiris the scribe Ani splendour in heaven, power upon earth, and triumph in the Other World. Grant that I may sail down to Tatu in the form of a living soul, and sail up to Abydos in the form of the Benu bird; that I may go in and come out without being stopped at the pylons of the Lords of the Other World. May there be given unto me bread-cakes in the house of coolness, and offerings of food in Anu (Heliopolis), and a homestead for ever in Sekhet Aru, with wheat and barley therefor.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV, the opening hymn to Osiris in the Papyrus of Ani.

title.en: The Machines of the Pyramid: Finished from the Top Downwards
title.zh: 金字塔之機：自頂而下成之

region.en: Giza, Egypt (the great pyramid of Cheops)
region.zh: 埃及吉薩（胡夫大金字塔）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.125 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 125

summary.en: The oldest account of pyramid engineering: 'they raised the remaining stones with machines made of short pieces of timber, raising them first from the ground to the first stage of the steps... for as many as were the courses of the steps, so many machines there were also, or perhaps they transferred one and the same machine... to each stage successively' — and the pyramid, Herodotus insists, 'was made after the manner of steps' and finished from the top downwards, with sixteen hundred talents of silver spent on radishes, onions and leeks for the workmen.
summary.zh: 金字塔工程之最古記載：『彼等以短木所製之機起餘石，先自地面升至第一層階台……階級有幾，機即有幾；或以一機遞轉於各層』——希羅多德力言塔為『階台式』，自頂而下而成；工友所食蘿蔔洋蔥韭蒜，銘文記耗銀一千六百他蘭同。

sensitivity.note: Ancient engineering-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Herodotus' machines are a literary tradition, not archaeology.

passages.text: This pyramid was made after the manner of steps, which some call 'rows' and others 'bases': and when they had first made it thus, they raised the remaining stones with machines made of short pieces of timber, raising them first from the ground to the first stage of the steps, and when the stone got up to this it was placed upon another machine standing on the first stage, and so from this it was drawn to the second upon another machine; for as many as were the courses of the steps, so many machines there were also, or perhaps they transferred one and the same machine, made so as easily to be carried, to each stage successively, in order that they might take up the stones.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.125.

passages.text: However that may be, the highest parts of it were finished first, and afterwards they proceeded to finish that which came next to them, and lastly they finished the parts of it near the ground and the lowest ranges. On the pyramid it is declared in Egyptian writing how much was spent on radishes and onions and leeks for the workmen, and if I rightly remember that which the interpreter said in reading to me this inscription, a sum of one thousand six hundred talents of silver was spent.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.125.
